x_lr_children_hl: Children live with households aged 26 to 50. Across those ages the reform moves homelessness in opposite directions: it falls by $2$ percent among households aged 26 to 34, rises by $2$ percent at 35 to 44 and falls by $1$ percent at 45 to 50. The changes cancel out almost exactly. Which way it goes at a given age depends on the balance of the two forces above. Treatment First cuts the number of households with a SUD, but raises the risk of homelessness for those who still have one, because they lose their voucher. At 26 to 34 the first force wins. The share of households with a SUD falls from $5.59$ to $3.83$ percent, while the share of them who are homeless rises only from $2.27$ to $2.59$ percent. So homelessness at these ages falls from $0.93$ to $0.91$ percent. This is because a disorder acquired young has not had enough time to cost most of these households their jobs, so few of them depend on a voucher to stay housed. At 35 to 44 the second force wins. The share with a SUD falls by about as much, from $6.61$ to $4.38$ percent, but these households have carried the disorder longer, and more of them have lost their jobs and depend on a voucher. Without the vouchers, the share of them who are homeless rises from $4.55$ to $7.36$ percent, so homelessness at these ages rises from $1.22$ to $1.25$ percent. At 45 to 50 the second force is stronger still. The SUD figures are by ten-year band, and across ages 45 to 54 the share of households with a SUD who are homeless rises from $3.72$ to $7.59$ percent. But at these ages the vouchers the reform revokes do more for everyone else. They go to other clean and eligible households, and homelessness among households without a SUD falls from $0.66$ to $0.57$ percent, against almost no change at younger ages. Together with the fall in the share with a SUD, from $4.78$ to $3.13$ percent, this outweighs the second force, so homelessness at 45 to 50 falls, by $1$ percent.
